newsitem.title: HAITI: Preval's first year seen as quasi-success in Haiti.
newsitem.headline: Preval's first year seen as quasi-success in Haiti.

text.p: One year ago, Haiti's capital was a scene of pomp and circumstance, filled with dignitaries marking the county's first peaceful transition of power from one freely elected leader to another.
Since President Rene Preval's inauguration last Feb. 7, he has endured harsh criticism from a population that still lives in dire poverty, has a high illiteracy rate and violent crime.
The fact that Preval survived his first year at all in one of the most turbulent offices in the Western Hemisphere is seen by some analysts as an achievement in itself.
"On the positive side, power is still in place," said a column on Friday in Le Nouvelliste newspaper.

In the past 10 years, Haiti has seen 10 changes in its presidency, including Preval's inauguration and Jean-Bertrand Aristide's restoration to power following three years in exile after a 1991 military coup.
Friday was also the 10th anniversary of the departure of Jean-Claude Duvalier, which ended a 29-year family dynasty of dictatorship in Haiti passed on by Francois Duvalier.
In the first months of Preval's term, there was a series of unsolved attacks on police officers and in recent weeks the country has been hit by often violent clashes between protesters and police.
Preval defends his public record, saying the groundwork has been laid for improvements and that it takes time to overhaul a nation.

"In one year, it is nearly impossible to effect big change," he told residents this week of Cite Soleil, a huge slum in Port-au-Prince with a population estimated to include 200,000 of Haiti's very poorest. "The day we plant is not the day we harvest," he said during the inauguration of a badly needed potable water storage house in the slum.
What could be Preval's most significant achievement is also among his least popular.

The 54-year-old president, who succeeded Aristide, has focused much of his first year preparing for the privatisation of nine government-run businesses, including the telephone and electricity companies, and Port-au-Prince's port and airport.

A law allowing joint ventures, management contracts and concessions to speed up the transition to private hands was approved last fall by the often uncooperative parliament. However, the pace is still seen as too slow by international donors who have tied aid to concrete steps on privatisation.
Preval has also touted progress on road and irrigation projects and promised that funds from privatisation would help pay for more infrastructure improvement.
But the starving population is growing increasingly impatient. Haiti's per capita income is still $250 per year, the hemisphere's lowest.

In addition, grass-roots organisations claim privatisation is tailored more to the expectations of foreign donors than to the needs of the masses. Aristide, who had popular support, added fuel to the fire by speaking out against privatisation.
The privatisation process started and was then abandoned after 20,000 international troops restored Aristide to power in October 1994. U.N. troops still patrol Haiti's streets.
Preval, an agronomist by training, spent the anniversary of his inauguration on Friday touring farmland.

Some Haitians praise Preval's hard-working image, focusing their criticism on Prime Minister Rosny Smarth and crediting the president with trying to make changes. "We voted for Preval and we know he is out there, at least he is doing something," said one protester at a demonstration last month.
